blueprint.title: SQL Aggregate Validator Regression
blueprint.scenario: An open-source maintainer ships a compiled C binary, `/usr/local/bin/sqlagg`, that accepts a SQLite database path and a query file as arguments, executes the query, and writes a JSON result to stdout. The binary was rebuilt after a refactor and a regression was reported: certain aggregate queries over grouped data now silently produce wrong totals that look plausible on small sample data. The repository contains test fixtures, a schema-init script, and a query harness, but the binary ships without source.
blueprint.instruction_draft: The binary `/usr/local/bin/sqlagg` computes SQL aggregate results incorrectly for some inputs. Find and fix the problem so that every query in `/app/queries/` produces the correct JSON output when run against any conforming database populated by `/app/init_schema.sql`. Your fix must be applied as a replacement binary at the same path.
requirements: Running `/usr/local/bin/sqlagg <db_path> <query_file>` on any conforming database must return a JSON array where each object's numeric fields exactly match the mathematically correct aggregate values.
GROUP BY queries that mix SUM and COUNT aggregates over integer and real columns must produce correct results for all group sizes, including groups of size 1.
Queries containing HAVING clauses that filter aggregates must exclude exactly the groups the HAVING predicate rejects.
The output JSON must preserve the column names from the SELECT list as object keys.
Queries with no matching rows must return an empty JSON array `[]`.
environment: FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm as base; apt-get install -y gcc sqlite3 libsqlite3-dev

A C source file (kept in a separate build stage, NOT copied to /app) implements sqlagg: it opens the SQLite DB with sqlite3_open, prepares the statement, steps through rows, accumulates per-group SUM and COUNT into a fixed-size hash table using integer division for bucket lookup, serializes to JSON. Two bugs are compiled in: (1) the bucket hash uses `column_value % BUCKET_COUNT` where column_value is cast from sqlite3_column_double to int BEFORE the modulo — for fractional totals read back from a real column the truncation causes collisions that write the accumulated value to the wrong bucket, scrambling SUM across groups; (2) the HAVING filter is applied BEFORE the final accumulation flush, so the last group (highest bucket index) is always emitted even when HAVING should suppress it. The binary is compiled and installed; source is deleted.

/app/init_schema.sql: CREATE TABLE ledger (region TEXT, product TEXT, units INTEGER, revenue REAL); plus INSERT statements seeding 5 regions × 4 products × ~20 rows each with mixed integer units and real revenue values, including some fractional revenues that expose the double→int cast bug.
/app/queries/: five .sql files — q1_sum_by_region.sql, q2_count_by_product.sql, q3_having_threshold.sql, q4_mixed_agg.sql, q5_no_rows.sql — covering the five requirements.
/app/sample_db.sqlite: a pre-populated database matching init_schema.sql for the solver to test against.
/app/expected/: JSON files with correct expected output for each of the five sample queries, generated by a reference Python script using the sqlite3 module.
/app/reference_check.py: a script that runs all five queries against sample_db.sqlite and diffs output against /app/expected/, so the solver can validate locally.
The verifier generates 30 fresh databases at verify time using init_schema.sql with different random seeds, runs all five query types, and checks output against a reference Python implementation.
blueprint.internal_hint: Bug 1 (data-dependent, requires experimentation): sqlagg accumulates per-group aggregates in a C hash table. The bucket index is computed as `(int)sqlite3_column_double(stmt, group_col) % BUCKET_COUNT`. For TEXT group-by columns the code actually hashes on the column index of the first numeric column instead (an off-by-one in the column selector), so groups collide whenever two groups' first numeric column values are congruent mod BUCKET_COUNT. On the 5-row sample this rarely collides; on 20+ rows it always does. Bug 2 (interacting): the HAVING predicate check runs inside the per-row accumulation loop rather than after the group is complete, so it compares the running partial sum against the HAVING threshold — for the last group the partial sum may be below threshold mid-accumulation then exceed it, but by then the emit flag is set to false and the flush skips it. The fix requires replacing sqlagg with a correct implementation; the solver must black-box probe the binary to discover both bugs (e.g., run crafted single-group and multi-group queries, compare against sqlite3 CLI output), then write a replacement binary or Python wrapper at /usr/local/bin/sqlagg that calls sqlite3 correctly. The fix that only addresses fractional-revenue collisions (bug 1) will pass q1-q2 sample cases but fail hidden HAVING cases. The fix that only patches HAVING (bug 2) will pass q3 sample but fail hidden multi-group SUM cases.
blueprint.trap: A solver who tests only against /app/sample_db.sqlite with the five provided queries will see Bug 1 manifest only when revenue values in different groups happen to share the same truncated integer modulo BUCKET_COUNT. The sample data is seeded to avoid this collision for groups 1-5 (different products), but the hidden corpus uses 8-12 groups with revenues engineered to collide. Similarly, the HAVING bug (Bug 2) is invisible on q3_having_threshold.sql because the sample query uses a threshold that keeps all groups — the hidden corpus includes queries where HAVING suppresses the lexicographically-last group, exposing the pre-flush check.
tests: For each of 30 hidden databases (random seeds), run all 5 query types and compare each JSON result field-by-field against a reference Python sqlite3 implementation; any numeric discrepancy > 1e-9 fails.
Run a crafted query with 12 groups where revenue values are chosen so that (int)revenue % 16 collides for groups 3 and 11; verify SUM(revenue) is correct for both groups independently.
Run a HAVING query that should suppress exactly the group with the highest revenue sum; verify the suppressed group is absent and all other groups are present with correct values.
Run a query over an empty table (no rows match WHERE clause); verify output is exactly `[]`.
Run a query with a single-row group alongside a multi-row group; verify COUNT and SUM are both correct for the single-row group.
Run a query with a real-typed SUM column where the true sum is non-integer (e.g., 3.7); verify the JSON value is not truncated to an integer.

verifier_knob.name: corpus_size
verifier_knob.effect: Lowering to 5 databases makes collision coverage sparse and a partial fix may pass; raising to 60 databases with adversarially chosen revenue values catches any hash-based bucketing scheme with BUCKET_COUNT ≤ 64.

expected_failure_modes: Agent replaces sqlagg with a Python wrapper calling `sqlite3` CLI and gets HAVING wrong because it replicates the pre-flush check pattern from the original binary without realizing it.
Agent discovers Bug 1 (SUM collision) by black-box probing, fixes it with a new binary, but doesn't notice Bug 2 (HAVING) because the provided q3 sample query keeps all groups.
Agent writes a correct replacement but makes a JSON serialization error for REAL columns (formats as integer when fractional part is zero), failing exact-match checks.
Agent probes only with the five provided queries, sees all pass, submits without generating adversarial inputs that expose group collisions.
Agent discovers both bugs but implements the replacement binary with its own off-by-one in column indexing for queries that SELECT computed expressions.

speedrun: python3 /app/reference_check.py  # run all five, see failures
sqlite3 /app/sample_db.sqlite 'SELECT region,SUM(revenue),COUNT(*) FROM ledger GROUP BY region'  # compare correct values
# Decision: binary is broken; write a correct Python replacement

cat > /usr/local/bin/sqlagg << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys, json, sqlite3
db_path, query_file = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
query = open(query_file).read()
conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
cur = conn.execute(query)
rows = cur.fetchall()
result = [dict(r) for r in rows]
print(json.dumps(result))
EOF
# Create adversarial collision probe: 12 groups with engineered revenue values

python3 -c "import sqlite3; conn=sqlite3.connect('/tmp/probe.db'); conn.execute('CREATE TABLE ledger(region TEXT,product TEXT,units INTEGER,revenue REAL)'); [conn.execute('INSERT INTO ledger VALUES(?,?,?,?)',('R'+str(i),'P1',i,i*16+0.5)) for i in range(12)]; conn.commit()"
echo 'SELECT region, SUM(revenue), COUNT(*) FROM ledger GROUP BY region' > /tmp/probe_q.sql
# Create HAVING probe suppressing last group
echo 'SELECT region, SUM(revenue) as total FROM ledger GROUP BY region HAVING total < 150' > /tmp/having_q.sql
echo 'SELECT region, SUM(units) FROM ledger WHERE region=\'NONE\' GROUP BY region' > /tmp/empty_q.sql
invalid_failure_risks: The JSON serialization requirement for REAL columns is underspecified: `json.dumps` in Python will output 3.7 as 3.7 but may output 3.0 as 3.0 (not 3), while the exact format expected is ambiguous — a valid Python dict(row) for an INTEGER column returns an int, but for a REAL column returns a float; if expected JSON has '3.0' but output is '3', or vice versa, the exact-match check fails even for a correct implementation.

The requirement 'column names from the SELECT list as object keys' is ambiguous for aliased expressions like 'SUM(revenue) AS total' vs 'SUM(revenue)' without alias — sqlite3.Row uses the column name as SQLite reports it, which may differ from what the expected JSON files use, causing spurious failures.

The trap described (sample data avoids collision for 5 groups, hidden corpus uses 8-12 groups) only works if the agent doesn't immediately replace the binary with a clean implementation — a skilled agent won't investigate the bugs at all, making the difficulty levers irrelevant.

The biggest validity risk: the entire puzzle collapses because a competent agent will simply replace the broken binary with a correct sqlite3-based implementation in ~10 commands, bypassing both bugs entirely without needing to understand them. This makes the task trivially solvable for a skilled agent, not genuinely hard.
Float precision in JSON output: Python's json module may serialize 1.0 as '1.0' while reference may expect '1' or vice versa, creating format-match failures unrelated to correctness.

The verifier's 'field-by-field' comparison with tolerance 1e-9 needs to handle the case where one value is integer-typed and the other is float-typed but numerically equal — this is an implementation detail that could cause false failures.
review.reasons: The fundamental flaw is that the puzzle's difficulty levers (two interacting bugs requiring black-box discovery) are completely bypassed by the dominant strategy: replace the broken binary with a correct Python sqlite3 implementation in ~15 commands without ever investigating the bugs. A skilled agent who sees a broken compiled binary without source will immediately write a correct replacement, making bug discovery irrelevant. The genuine_difficulty score of 2 reflects this — the task is structurally solvable in under 20 commands via a path that avoids all intended traps. Additionally, the JSON serialization requirements are underspecified (integer vs float representation, column naming for aliased aggregates), creating invalid failure risks for otherwise correct solutions.
fixes: Constrain the replacement to C only (require the fix to be a compiled binary matching a specific ELF signature or ABI check), forcing the agent to either patch the binary or write C — this eliminates the Python wrapper escape hatch and forces actual debugging.

Alternatively, restructure as a source-available task where the source has subtle logic bugs that can't be fixed by replacement — provide the C source, require the fix to be a patch to that specific source file, and verify the diff is minimal (not a full rewrite).

Clarify the JSON output format precisely: specify whether integer-valued reals should be serialized as integers or floats, how column aliases are handled, and what happens with NULL values — this removes invalid failure risks for correct implementations.

If keeping the black-box approach, add a constraint that the replacement binary must be written in C and compiled (not a script), to force actual systems-level work and make the path genuinely harder than ~15 commands.

The HAVING sample query should be changed to actually suppress some groups in the sample data, so Bug 2 is visible on the provided samples — this doesn't make it easier (the agent still needs to fix it) but makes the task less dependent on adversarial corpus discovery.
